etymology: From the preposition by doubled and used adverbially in older English to mean “in close order, one hard upon another,” and so “straightway, at once”; the modern sense of “after a while, eventually” is a later softening of the very same phrase.
biblical_def: By and by in the KJV does not mean “eventually,” as our ears now take it. It means immediately, at once, this very moment. The word is turned clean around: what once named the shortest interval now names a long one. Scripture will not let the mistake stand. When Herod’s dancing girl was prompted by her mother, she came in with haste and demanded, “I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist” (Mar 6:25) — not someday, but now, before the feast cooled and the king’s rash oath could cool with it. So too in the parable of the sower: the stony-ground hearer receives the word with joy, yet hath no root in himself, and when tribulation ariseth, “by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21) — his fall is not slow apostasy but instant collapse the moment the sun is up. And the Lord teaches the servant’s place with it: which of you will say to a servant come from the field, by and by, “Go and sit down to meat” (Luk 17:7)? The immediacy is the whole point. Yet the same phrase can sound a sober warning: of wars and commotions the Lord says “the end is not by and by” (Luk 21:9) — not immediately, whatever the alarmists cry. The reader who softens by and by into “presently, in time” loses the very urgency the Holy Ghost pressed into it.
webster_summary: Immediately; at once; straightway — not, as now, “after a while.”
webster_full: BY AND BY, immediately; at once; without delay.
From by repeated, in the old sense of “in close order, one hard upon another.”
The modern “after a while, presently” is a later weakening of the phrase.
The dancer asked the Baptist’s head “by and by” — that instant (Mar 6:25).
The stony hearer is offended “by and by” — the moment trouble comes (Mat 13:21).
scriptures: Mar 6:25
And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
Luk 17:7
But which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding cattle, will say unto him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go and sit down to meat?
Luk 21:9
But when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by.
corruption_summary: A word turned inside out: the AV’s “by and by” means now, while ours means later — and the urgency is lost with the change.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a genuine reversal of sense, and it must be named, for it misleads every modern reader of the Gospels. In the Authorized Version “by and by” means immediately; in our speech it means eventually, after a while, when we get round to it. The two are opposites. A reader who does not know it will picture the stony-ground hearer drifting slowly from the faith, when the Lord says he is offended by and by — the instant the heat rises. He will imagine Herod’s court taking its leisure over John, when the girl demanded the head that moment. The drift is not wicked, only worn: a phrase for the sharpest haste has been rubbed down into a phrase for delay.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the immediacy of God’s summons and man’s response. Scripture is full of now: today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts; behold, now is the accepted time. The stony hearer’s ruin was instant because his root was never there, and the sun that should have ripened him withered him instead. Against him stands the servant who obeys at once, and the Master who bids His own watch, for they know not the hour. The softening of “by and by” into “someday” is the very disease of the natural heart, which hears the call of God and answers, later. The word as the KJV meant it rebukes the delay: not by and by, but now.
roots_summary: The word means immediately, at once — the sharpest haste, not the leisured “eventually” of modern speech.
roots_lines: By and by — the preposition by doubled and used adverbially.
In older English it meant “in close succession,” hence “straightway, at once.”
The modern sense “after a while” is a weakening of the same phrase.
The dancer demanded the Baptist’s head by and by — that instant (Mar 6:25).
The stony hearer is offended by and by, the moment trouble comes (Mat 13:21).
usage: By and by means now, not later: the girl wanted John’s head that very moment.
“By and by he is offended” — the stony hearer falls at once, not by slow degrees.
“The end is not by and by”: not immediately, whatever the setters of dates may cry.

etymology: From present + -ly — “at the present instant”; in the KJV it keeps its first force, now, this moment. The modern “soon, in a little while” is a slackening of the word away from the very present it names.
biblical_def: Presently in the KJV means at once, this instant — not, as we now use it, “in a little while, soon enough.” The word still carries the present in it, and the AV means exactly that: now. When Peter drew a sword in the garden, the Lord rebuked the defence with a word of what He might have summoned: “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?” (Mat 26:53). Not after some delay of heaven — presently, the moment He asked, twelve legions and more would stand in the garden. He would not ask it, for the Scripture must be fulfilled and the cup drunk; but the power was instant. Paul uses it of his own plans: “Him therefore I hope to send presently, so soon as I shall see how it will go with me” (Php 2:23) — without delay, the moment the matter was clear. And the wise man marks the fool by his speed: “A fool’s wrath is presently known” (Pro 12:16), flaring out that instant, while a prudent man covereth shame. Set against these the corruption of Eli’s sons, who would not wait even for the fat to be burned but seized the flesh raw: “Let them not fail to burn the fat presently” (1Sa 2:16). The word names the sharpest immediacy, and to read it as “by and by, eventually” is to blunt every text it enters.
webster_summary: At once; immediately; this instant — not the modern “soon, in a little while.”
webster_full: PRESENTLY, at present; immediately; without delay.
From present, “the instant now”; the sense has since slackened to “soon.”
In the KJV it always means at once, never “after a while.”
Christ could presently have twelve legions of angels — that instant (Mat 26:53).
A fool’s wrath is presently known, flaring out at once (Pro 12:16).
scriptures: Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?
Php 2:23
Him therefore I hope to send presently, so soon as I shall see how it will go with me.
A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame.

And if any man said unto him, Let them not fail to burn the fat presently, and then take as much as thy soul desireth; then he would answer him, Nay; but thou shalt give it me now: and if not, I will take it by force.
corruption_summary: An honest drift: the AV’s “presently” means now, ours means soon — the word has drifted from the present it is named for.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is quiet but real, and it dulls the reader’s ear. “Presently” once meant at this present moment; now it means in a little while, and the change robs the Gospel of its force. When the Lord says He could presently have twelve legions of angels, He does not mean heaven would send them after some interval — He means the instant He asked. A reader who hears the modern “soon” imagines a delay where the text asserts an omnipotent immediacy, and so misses the majesty of the restraint: the power was wholly present, and He would not use it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the instant sufficiency of God. He does not need time to gather His resources; twelve legions of angels wait upon a word, and the cup was drunk not from weakness but from love. The same immediacy searches the heart: a fool’s wrath is presently known, betraying him that moment, while the prudent covereth shame — grace is patient where nature is quick. Let the believer learn from the word what he loses in the drift: God’s help is never late, and His restraint is never impotence. What He could do presently, He forbears to do only that a greater purpose stand.
roots_summary: The word means at once, this present instant — not the modern, slackened “soon.”
roots_lines: Presently — from present, “the instant now,” + -ly.
In the KJV it means at once, this very moment.
The modern “soon, in a little while” is a slackening of the sense.
Christ could presently have had twelve legions of angels (Mat 26:53).
A fool’s wrath is presently known — that instant (Pro 12:16).
usage: Presently means now: twelve legions would have stood in the garden that instant.
“I hope to send him presently” — Paul means without delay, not eventually.
A fool’s wrath is presently known: his anger flares the moment he is crossed.

etymology: From forth + with — “forth with” the moment, along with the very instant; hence immediately, straightway. The word keeps its plain force in modern legal English but is otherwise nearly lost.
biblical_def: Forthwith means immediately, straightway, that same moment — and here the modern reader is in less danger, for the word, though archaic, has not reversed. It is one of the KJV’s several renderings of the Greek adverbs of haste, and it drives the Gospel narratives forward. In the parable of the sower the seed on stony ground springs up forthwith, “because they had no deepness of earth” (Mat 13:5) — a quick, rootless growth that the sun as quickly scorches. When the Lord gave the unclean spirits leave, “forthwith Jesus gave them leave,” and the herd ran violently down into the sea (Mar 5:13); the permission and the plunge were of a moment. The traitor’s kiss is stamped with it: “forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him” (Mat 26:49) — no hesitation in the betrayal. And when the angel had led Peter through the wards and the iron gate, “forthwith the angel departed from him” (Act 12:10), the deliverance complete and the messenger gone in an instant. The word marks the swiftness of divine action and human deed alike: seed springing, swine drowning, a kiss given, an angel vanishing. Scripture moves at the pace of forthwith; the God who speaks and it is done does not dawdle, and the events of redemption crowd one upon another, each following its cause without a breath between.
webster_full: FORTHWITH, immediately; without delay; directly.
From forth and with — “forth with” the very moment.
It renders the Greek adverbs of instant action in the Gospels.
The stony seed sprang up forthwith and as quickly withered (Mat 13:5).
When Peter was free, forthwith the angel departed from him (Act 12:10).
scriptures: Mat 13:5
Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth:
Mar 5:13

And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.

When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him.
corruption_summary: An archaic but unturned word for immediacy; it recovers the breathless pace at which Scripture reports the acts of God and men.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no reversal to warn against here, only a fading: “forthwith” is nearly gone from common speech, kept alive chiefly in the language of the law, where a thing done forthwith must be done at once and not at leisure. The KJV uses it just so. The danger is not misreading but skimming — the modern eye slides over the little adverb and misses how much of the Gospel it carries. Forthwith the seed sprang; forthwith Christ gave leave; forthwith the betrayer kissed; forthwith the angel departed. Strike the word out and the narrative loses its pulse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the swiftness of God’s working. He said, Let there be light, and there was light; He speaks and it is done, He commandeth and it standeth fast. The adverbs of haste that fill the Gospel of Mark are not an accident of style but a testimony: the kingdom of God came near in power, and the acts of the Lord followed His word without delay. The same speed will mark the end — in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, the trumpet shall sound. The believer who reads “forthwith” rightly reads a God who does not procrastinate, whose promises are not slack, and whose salvation, when its hour is come, forthwith arrives.
roots_summary: The word means immediately, straightway, that same instant.
roots_lines: Forthwith — from forth + with, “forth with” the moment.
It means immediately, without delay; the legal sense preserves it still.
It renders the Gospel’s Greek adverbs of instant action.
The stony seed sprang up forthwith, then withered (Mat 13:5).
Forthwith the delivering angel departed from Peter (Act 12:10).
usage: Forthwith means at once: the stony seed sprang up that moment and as fast was scorched.
“Forthwith he came to Jesus… and kissed him” — the betrayal without a pause.
When the deliverance was done, forthwith the angel departed — his errand ended in an instant.

etymology: From straight (“direct, without bending”) + way; hence “by a direct way,” and so immediately, at once. It is not strait (“narrow”) but straight (“direct”) — the way that goes right on without turning aside.
biblical_def: Straightway means immediately, at once, on the instant — and the modern reader must not confuse the straight in it (direct, unbending) with the strait that means narrow. To go straightway is to go by the direct road, without turning or tarrying. It is the signature word of Mark’s Gospel, which hurries from deed to deed. At the baptism, “straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened” (Mar 1:10); Matthew tells the same: Jesus “went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him” (Mat 3:16). The heavens did not wait; the moment the Son rose from Jordan they were rent. So the Lord’s ministry begins: “straightway on the sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, and taught” (Mar 1:21), no interval between arrival and teaching. And so conversion works: when Saul was changed on the Damascus road, “straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God” (Act 9:20) — not after years of seasoning, but at once, the new heart declaring itself the moment it was given. The word teaches an immediacy that belongs to grace. When God acts, the heavens open straightway; when God calls, the fishermen leave their nets and follow straightway; when God converts, the persecutor preaches straightway. There is a promptness in the works of the Spirit that the loitering heart of nature knows nothing of, and “straightway” is its watchword.
webster_summary: Immediately; at once; by a direct course — from straight (“direct”), not strait (“narrow”).
webster_full: STRAIGHTWAY, immediately; without loss of time; at once.
From straight (“direct”) + way: by a direct course, without turning aside.
It is not strait, “narrow”; the two words are often confused.
Straightway from Jordan the heavens were opened to the Son (Mar 1:10).
Converted Saul straightway preached Christ in the synagogues (Act 9:20).
scriptures: Mar 1:10
And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him:
Mat 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
Mar 1:21
And they went into Capernaum; and straightway on the sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, and taught.
Act 9:20
And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.
corruption_summary: An unreversed word for immediacy, easily confused with strait; it recovers the promptness that marks the works of the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: The one trap in this word is the eye, not the age: straightway is built on straight, “direct,” and not on strait, “narrow” — two words the KJV keeps distinct and the modern reader often merges. To go straightway is not to go by a narrow gate but by a direct road, and the force of it is temporal: at once, without a bend or a delay. Mark’s Gospel is stitched together with it, and to skim past the word is to miss the breathless pace at which he reports the coming of the kingdom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the promptness of grace. When the Spirit works, He works straightway: the heavens open the moment Christ rises from the water, the called disciple leaves his nets and follows, the converted persecutor mounts the pulpit at once. This is not the reluctant, deferred obedience of the natural man, who is forever meaning to repent and never doing it, but the swift response of a heart made new. Saul did not negotiate a slow retirement from his old life; straightway he preached the faith he once destroyed. Let the believer measure his own obedience by the word. God’s summons calls for a straightway answer, and delay is not deliberation but disobedience wearing its coat.
roots_summary: The word means immediately, at once, by a direct course — from straight, not strait.
roots_lines: Straightway — from straight (“direct”) + way.
It means immediately, by a direct road, without turning aside.
Not to be confused with strait, “narrow.”
Straightway the heavens opened to Christ at His baptism (Mar 1:10).
Converted Saul straightway preached Christ (Act 9:20).
usage: Straightway means at once: the heavens opened the instant Christ rose from Jordan.
“Straightway… he entered into the synagogue, and taught” — no pause before the work.
It is straight (direct), not strait (narrow): the way that goes right on without turning.

etymology: From hence (“from here, from this”) + forth (“forward”); hence “from this time forward, from now on.” It looks not backward but ahead, marking a line after which all is changed.
biblical_def: Henceforth means from this time forward — from now on. It is a word that draws a line across a life or a history and declares that after it nothing shall be as before. The modern reader is in little danger of reversing it, but great danger of skimming it, for on that little line hang some of the weightiest turns in Scripture. At the last supper the Lord sets the line at His death: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Mat 26:29). Paul sets it at the cross for our knowledge of Christ: “Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh” (2Co 5:16) — the old carnal reckoning ends, and a new estimate of every man begins. The Lord sets it at His own self-revealing: “from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him” (Joh 14:7) — the Father made visible in the Son from that hour on. And Paul sets it at our union with the crucified Christ: our old man is crucified with Him, “that henceforth we should not serve sin” (Rom 6:6). Mark that last well. Henceforth is the grammar of the new birth. There is a decisive before and after in the Christian’s life, and the believer lives on the far side of a line grace has drawn. What he was, he is no more; henceforth he is Christ’s.
webster_summary: From this time forward; from now on; from this point onward.
webster_full: HENCEFORTH, from this time forward; onward from the present.
From hence (“from this”) + forth (“forward”).
It looks ahead, marking a line after which all is changed.
Christ would drink no more of the vine henceforth, until the kingdom (Mat 26:29).
Crucified with Christ, henceforth we should not serve sin (Rom 6:6).
scriptures: But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom.
Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more.
Joh 14:7
If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him.
Rom 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
corruption_summary: A plain word for “from now on”; it recovers the decisive line grace draws between the old life and the new.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no corruption of sense to fight here, only the reader’s temptation to hurry past a small word that carries a large weight. “Henceforth” announces a dividing line: a before and an after, a point past which the terms of life are altered. When the Lord says He will drink no more of the vine henceforth until the kingdom, He is marking the eve of His death as a boundary. When Paul says henceforth we know no man after the flesh, he is dating a whole new way of seeing from the cross. Skim the word and the boundary vanishes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the decisive character of conversion. The gospel is not a gradual improvement of the old man but his crucifixion and the raising of a new: our old man is crucified with Christ, that henceforth we should not serve sin. There is a real line in the believer’s history — not always felt in a single moment, but true in fact — before which he was under sin’s dominion and after which he is not. This is the ground of all pursuit of holiness: not “become what you are not” by mere effort, but “be what you now are” in Christ. Reckon ye yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin. Henceforth is the word of a redeemed man, and it faces forward.
roots_summary: The word means from this time forward, from now on — a line after which all is changed.
roots_lines: Henceforth — hence (“from this”) + forth (“forward”).
It means from this time onward, and looks ahead, not back.
It marks a boundary past which the terms of life are altered.
Christ drinks no more of the vine henceforth, until the kingdom (Mat 26:29).
Crucified with Christ, henceforth the believer serves not sin (Rom 6:6).
usage: Henceforth means from now on: a line drawn across the life, changing all that follows.
“Henceforth know we no man after the flesh” — the old reckoning ends at the cross.
Crucified with Christ, the believer henceforth serves sin no more — a decisive before and after.

etymology: From hard + -ly; in older English “with hardness” — that is, with difficulty, or with severity, harshly. The modern sense “scarcely, almost not” is a later development that has all but swallowed the earlier one.
biblical_def: Hardly in the KJV does not mean “scarcely, almost not,” as we now use it, but with difficulty, or with severity, harshly. It is the adverb of hard: a thing done hardly is done with hardness, against resistance, at great cost. So the Lord’s solemn word on riches: “a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 19:23), and again, “How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!” (Mar 10:23). He does not mean the rich barely squeeze in; He means their entrance is a thing of great difficulty, so hard that with men it is impossible, and only the God with whom all things are possible can accomplish it. The word carries the sense of severity elsewhere: the foul spirit, tearing the child, “bruising him hardly departeth from him” (Luk 9:39) — it leaves only with violence, wounding as it goes. And it names the harsh estate of a people under judgment: they shall pass through the land “hardly bestead and hungry” (Isa 8:21), sore pressed and set upon by want. The reader who hears the modern “hardly” will soften the Lord’s warning into a near-miss, as though the rich almost fail to enter; but the truth is graver. Riches are a real and mighty hindrance to the soul, and the camel and the needle’s eye stand for a passage no wealth can make by itself.
webster_summary: With difficulty; with severity; harshly — not the modern “scarcely, almost not.”
webster_full: HARDLY, with difficulty; with severity; harshly; not easily.
From hard + -ly, “with hardness.”
The modern “scarcely, almost not” is a later sense that has nearly displaced it.
A rich man shall hardly — with great difficulty — enter the kingdom (Mat 19:23).
The foul spirit, bruising the child, hardly departed — only with violence (Luk 9:39).
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, Verily I say unto you, That a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven.
And Jesus looked round about, and saith unto his disciples, How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!
Luk 9:39
And, lo, a spirit taketh him, and he suddenly crieth out; and it teareth him that he foameth again, and bruising him hardly departeth from him.
Isa 8:21
And they shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: and it shall come to pass, that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and look upward.
corruption_summary: An honest drift: the AV’s “hardly” means with difficulty, ours means scarcely — and the Lord’s warning on riches is softened in the change.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is real, and it blunts a hard saying. In the KJV “hardly” means with difficulty; in our mouths it means scarcely, almost not. When the Lord says a rich man shall hardly enter the kingdom, the modern ear hears “the rich barely make it in,” a near thing but a thing accomplished. That is not His meaning. He means the entrance of the rich is a matter of the utmost difficulty — so hard that He follows it with the camel and the needle’s eye, and the disciples ask in astonishment, Who then can be saved? To read the softer word is to lose the astonishment, and with it the point.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the peril of riches and the power of God. Wealth is not a light thing to the soul; it roots a man in this world, feeds his self-sufficiency, and makes the narrow gate seem needless to one who wants for nothing. That is why the rich enter hardly. Yet the Lord does not shut the door: with men it is impossible, but with God all things are possible, and He has saved rich men and poor by the same sovereign grace. The word thus preaches two truths at once — the real difficulty that riches raise, and the greater power that overcomes it. Let no wealthy man presume, and let none despair; the camel passes the needle’s eye only by the hand of God.
roots_summary: The word means with difficulty, with severity, harshly — not the modern “scarcely.”
roots_lines: Hardly — from hard + -ly, “with hardness.”
It means with difficulty, or with severity, harshly.
The modern “scarcely, almost not” has nearly displaced the older sense.
A rich man shall hardly enter the kingdom — with great difficulty (Mat 19:23).
A people under judgment pass through hardly bestead and hungry (Isa 8:21).
usage: Hardly means with difficulty: the rich enter the kingdom hardly, not barely.
“How hardly shall they that have riches enter” — a passage as hard as the needle’s eye.
The foul spirit “bruising him hardly departeth”: it left the child only with violence.

etymology: From the Old French escars, “scanty, sparing,” from a Late Latin excarpsus, “plucked out, rare”; used adverbially it means scarcely, with difficulty, barely — a thing only just accomplished, and against resistance.
biblical_def: As an adverb, scarce (or scarcely) means with difficulty, barely, only just — the thing achieved, but hardly, against strong hindrance. Here modern usage has kept close to the old, yet the weight of the biblical texts repays attention. At Lystra, when the crowd would have offered sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas as gods, the apostles rent their clothes and reasoned with them, “and with these sayings scarce restrained they the people” (Act 14:18) — the mob was barely, with the utmost effort, held back from idolatry. On the voyage to Rome, sailing slowly against contrary winds, they “scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us” (Act 27:7) — the ship made the point only with great difficulty. But the deepest use is Peter’s, weighing the salvation of the righteous against the doom of the lost: “if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1Pe 4:18). Not that the saved are saved by a narrow margin of their own worth — but that salvation is a thing accomplished through fire, through much tribulation, at infinite cost, and no soul enters heaven cheaply. Paul reasons the same way of the cross: “scarcely for a righteous man will one die” (Rom 5:7), yet Christ died for the ungodly. The word measures the difficulty of the thing — and so magnifies the God who accomplished it when it could scarce be done at all.
webster_summary: With difficulty; barely; only just — a thing accomplished against strong hindrance.
webster_full: SCARCE (adv.), hardly; scarcely; with difficulty; only just.
From Old French escars, “scanty, sparing,” hence “rare, only just.”
It names a thing barely done, against strong resistance.
The apostles scarce restrained the crowd from sacrificing to them (Act 14:18).
If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly appear? (1Pe 4:18).
scriptures: And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them.
And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?
Rom 5:7
For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.
Act 27:7
And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone;
corruption_summary: An adverb little changed in sense; its texts recover how dearly salvation is bought — the righteous are saved, but scarcely, and never cheaply.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no reversal of meaning here to correct; the modern “scarcely” still means barely, with difficulty, and the KJV’s “scarce” is the same word older-dressed. What wants recovering is the weight of the texts. When Peter says the righteous are scarcely saved, careless readers have made him say the elect only just scrape in, as though salvation hung on a hair. His point is not the insecurity of the saved but the costliness of the saving: the way lies through fire and much tribulation, and if such a passage is required even for the righteous, the case of the ungodly is past all hope.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salvation is precious because it was hard. Not hard for God to purpose — His counsel stands — but hard in the doing: it cost the blood of His Son, and it brings the saved through affliction and fire. “Scarcely for a righteous man will one die,” Paul marvels, and then sets against that reluctance the wonder of the gospel: while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. The word rebukes every cheap and easy religion that promises heaven at no cost and by no cross. The righteous are saved — certainly, eternally — but scarcely, through much tribulation, and the crown is set upon a head that has known the fire.
roots_summary: As an adverb the word means barely, with difficulty, only just — a thing accomplished against hindrance.
roots_lines: Scarce — Old French escars, “scanty, sparing, rare.”
As an adverb it means barely, with difficulty, only just.
It names a thing done against strong resistance and at cost.
The apostles scarce restrained the crowd at Lystra (Act 14:18).
If the righteous scarcely be saved, where the ungodly? (1Pe 4:18).
usage: Scarce means with difficulty: the apostles scarce held the crowd back from idolatry.
“If the righteous scarcely be saved” — not by a narrow margin, but through fire.
The ship scarce came over against Cnidus — only just, against the wind.

etymology: From hither (“to this”) + to; but where hither is of place — “to this spot” — hitherto is of time: “up to this point, until now.” The two must not be confounded.
biblical_def: Hitherto means up to now, until this time — and here a careful distinction must be kept, for the word looks like hither but does not mean it. Hither is of place: “come hither” is come to this spot. Hitherto is of time: it reaches back over all that is past and brings it up to the present moment. So the Lord defends His sabbath healing: “My Father worketh hitherto, and I work” (Joh 5:17) — the Father has been working, without ceasing, from creation until now, and the Son works with Him. The word is often the voice of gratitude looking back. Samuel raised his stone of remembrance and named it Ebenezer, “saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1Sa 7:12) — every past mercy gathered up into one thankful monument. The children of Joseph plead their increase: “the LORD hath blessed me hitherto” (Jos 17:14), all the way to that day. And the porters of the temple are marked as those who “hitherto waited in the king’s gate eastward” (1Ch 9:18), faithful in their charge up to the time of writing. The word teaches the saint to read his whole past as a story of help. Hitherto — over every year and every trouble — the LORD has helped; and the God who has been Ebenezer thus far will not fail the little way that remains. What is behind is the pledge of what lies ahead.
webster_summary: Up to this time; until now — of time, not of place (which is hither).
webster_full: HITHERTO, to this time; until now; up to the present.
From hither + to; but the sense is temporal, not local.
Hither is “to this place”; hitherto is “up to this time.”
“My Father worketh hitherto, and I work” — from creation until now (Joh 5:17).
Samuel’s Ebenezer: hitherto hath the LORD helped us (1Sa 7:12).
scriptures: Joh 5:17
But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
And the children of Joseph spake unto Joshua, saying, Why hast thou given me but one lot and one portion to inherit, seeing I am a great people, forasmuch as the LORD hath blessed me hitherto?
Who hitherto waited in the king's gate eastward: they were porters in the companies of the children of Levi.
Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
corruption_summary: A temporal word easily confused with the local hither; it recovers the saint’s backward look of gratitude — hitherto the LORD hath helped.
corruption_paragraphs: The trap in this word is not the age but the eye and ear: hitherto is so like hither that the two are readily confounded, yet they belong to different worlds. Hither is a word of place — come hither, bring it hither, to this spot. Hitherto is a word of time — up to this moment, until now. When the Lord says His Father worketh hitherto, He is not speaking of a place the Father has come to but of the unbroken labour of God from creation to the present hour. Confuse the two and the sense collapses.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of the backward look. Scripture teaches the saint to gather up his past into a monument of praise: Samuel set his stone and called it Ebenezer — hitherto hath the LORD helped us — not naming one deliverance only, but all of them, up to that day. This is the cure for the fearful heart. The God who has been our help in ages past, who has brought us over every flood hitherto, does not change and does not tire; His arm is not shortened for the road that remains. Faith reads the whole story of the past as help, and from that reading draws its courage for the future. Raise your Ebenezer, and go on.
roots_summary: The word means up to this time, until now — of time, whereas hither is of place.
roots_lines: Hitherto — hither (“to this”) + to.
But its sense is temporal: “up to this time, until now.”
Hither is of place; hitherto is of time — do not confound them.
“My Father worketh hitherto” — from creation until now (Joh 5:17).
Hitherto hath the LORD helped us: Samuel’s Ebenezer (1Sa 7:12).
usage: Hitherto means until now: “My Father worketh hitherto” — from creation to this hour.
“Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” — the whole past gathered into one stone of thanks.
Mind the difference: hither is to this place; hitherto is up to this time.

etymology: From the Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding together, restraining oneself” (from continere, “to hold in”); hence without self-restraint, unable to hold oneself in. The modern narrowing to a bodily infirmity has all but hidden the moral sense the KJV intends.
biblical_def: Incontinent in the KJV is a word of the will, not of the body. It means without self-control, unrestrained, unable to hold oneself in — the man who has no rule over his appetites and passions. The modern ear hears only the bodily infirmity the word has since come to name, but Paul means a moral ruin. Cataloguing the marks of the last days, he lists the men from whom the godly must turn away: “without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). The incontinent man stands in that grim company because his sin is the same root as theirs — a self given wholly over to itself, ungoverned, spilling out in every direction. The wise man had drawn his picture long before: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls” (Pro 25:28) — defenceless, open to every enemy, because the inner restraint is gone. Against this stands the fruit of the Spirit, whose last-named grace is the very opposite: “temperance” — self-control — “against such there is no law” (Gal 5:23). And the runner in the games is Paul’s living emblem of it: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things” (1Co 9:25), disciplining body and desire to win a corruptible crown, that we might win an incorruptible. Continence is not native to fallen man; it is the Spirit’s gift and the saint’s daily discipline.
webster_summary: Without self-restraint; unable to govern one’s appetites and passions — a moral fault, not the modern bodily sense.
webster_full: INCONTINENT, unrestrained; not governing the appetites; lacking self-control.
From Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding oneself in.”
The KJV means a moral want of restraint, not the later bodily sense.
Paul lists the incontinent among the marks of the last days (2Ti 3:3).
Its opposite is temperance, the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23).
scriptures: Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
Gal 5:23
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
corruption_summary: A moral word narrowed to a bodily one; it recovers self-control as the Spirit’s fruit and the mark that parts the disciplined saint from the ungoverned world.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here has hidden a moral word behind a medical one. To modern ears “incontinent” names a bodily infirmity and nothing more; a man is not blamed for it, and rightly so where it is mere weakness of the flesh. But Paul’s word is not of the body but of the will. His incontinent man is the man without self-command — ungoverned in appetite, temper, and tongue — and he is named among trucebreakers and false accusers, not among the sick. To read the modern sense into 2Ti 3:3 is to turn a charge of sin into a note of misfortune, and to miss that the apostle is describing a generation in love with its own unrestraint.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that self-control is a Christian grace, not a natural gift. Fallen man is by nature a city broken down and without walls, his passions loose and his spirit unruled; and an age that bids every man follow his desires and never deny himself only tears the last stones from the wall. Scripture says the opposite. Temperance is the fruit of the Spirit; the runner in the games is temperate in all things; and he that ruleth his own spirit is stronger than he that taketh a city. Continence is won, not inherited — wrought in the believer by the Spirit and pursued by daily discipline. The incontinent life is not freedom but a ruin open to every enemy; the governed life, under God, is the only liberty.
roots_summary: The word means without self-restraint, ungoverned in appetite and passion — a moral fault, not the modern bodily one.
roots_lines: Incontinent — Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding in.”
It means without self-control, unable to hold oneself in.
The KJV sense is moral; the modern bodily sense is a later narrowing.
Paul lists the incontinent among the perilous men of the last days (2Ti 3:3).
Its opposite, temperance, is the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23).
usage: Incontinent means without self-control: Paul names it among the sins of the last days.
The incontinent man “hath no rule over his own spirit” — a city broken down and without walls.
Against the incontinent stands the runner, temperate in all things for an incorruptible crown.

etymology: From the Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase” (kin to the German wachsen and the Latin augere); the verb has no kinship with the wax of the honeycomb or the candle, which is a wholly different word. To wax is to grow, to become, to increase.
biblical_def: To wax, in the KJV, is to grow — to increase, to become. The modern reader knows the noun (the wax of bees and candles) and has all but lost the ancient verb, which is a different word altogether and means simply to grow greater in some quality or state. Scripture uses it constantly, and always of a becoming. It waxes cold: in the last days, “because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Mat 24:12) — charity does not vanish at a stroke but grows colder by degrees as sin multiplies. It waxes strong: of John the Baptist, “the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit” (Luk 1:80), the inward man increasing as the outward grew. It waxes valiant: the heroes of faith, “out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens” (Heb 11:34) — faith making the feeble grow into the bold. And it waxes hot with wrath: at the golden calf the LORD said to Moses, “let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them” (Exo 32:10) — the anger of God kindling and rising against a people’s sin. The word is a barometer of the soul and of the age. Love waxes cold, or faith waxes strong; wrath waxes hot, or the child of God waxes valiant. Whither a man is growing — colder or stronger — is the whole question, for wax he must; nothing in the living soul stands still.
webster_summary: To grow; to increase; to become — the archaic verb, wholly distinct from the wax of comb or candle.
webster_full: WAX (verb), to grow; to increase; to become; to pass into a state.
From Old English weaxan, “to grow,” kin to German wachsen.
It has no kinship with wax, the substance of comb and candle.
In the last days the love of many shall wax cold (Mat 24:12).
The heroes of faith waxed valiant in fight (Heb 11:34).
scriptures: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
Luk 1:80
And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.
Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.
Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation.
corruption_summary: An archaic verb eclipsed by an unrelated noun; it recovers that the soul is always becoming — love waxing cold or faith waxing strong, but never standing still.
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion here is not of meaning but of words: wax the verb and wax the noun are two separate words that happen to be spelled alike. The one is the honeycomb’s and the candle’s; the other, older and now nearly lost, means to grow, to become. A reader who knows only the substance may stumble at “the love of many shall wax cold” or “my wrath may wax hot,” as though wax could be cold or hot — but the verb has nothing to do with beeswax. To wax cold is to grow cold; to wax hot is to grow hot; to wax strong is to grow strong.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the soul is never static. The verb wax is always a becoming, and Scripture applies it to the deepest movements of the heart: love waxing cold as iniquity abounds, faith waxing strong out of weakness, the wrath of God waxing hot against sin. There is no standing still in the inner man; he is forever growing warmer or colder, stronger or weaker, toward Christ or away from Him. The believer cannot coast, for a love not waxing strong is already waxing cold, and the abounding iniquity of the last days is precisely the frost that cools it. Watch, therefore, which way you wax. The child that waxed strong in spirit and the heroes that waxed valiant in fight grew so by the grace that never leaves the soul at rest.
roots_summary: The archaic verb means to grow, to increase, to become — unrelated to the wax of comb or candle.
roots_lines: Wax (verb) — Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase.”
It means to grow, to become, to pass into a state or quality.
It is unrelated to wax, the substance of comb and candle.
In the last days the love of many shall wax cold (Mat 24:12).
The child John grew, and waxed strong in spirit (Luk 1:80).
usage: To wax means to grow: “the love of many shall wax cold” — grow cold by degrees.
“My wrath may wax hot” — the anger of God kindling and rising, not beeswax.
The heroes of faith waxed valiant — grew bold — out of weakness (Heb 11:34).
